text.p01: To everyone who ever rushed ahead: the old paths still have songs to teach. A story about learning from those who came before.
text.p03: In a green forest lived Ama, a young pangolin with shiny scales like a pinecone and one golden scale on the tip of her tail.
text.p04: Ama loved new things best of all: new paths, new games, new ways through the trees. "Look!" she'd shout. "I found a new way!"
text.p05: Every evening, Nana tapped her tail on a hollow log by the old silk-cotton tree. Katum, ka-tum. And she sang her old song:
text.p06: "Three round stones, then the bent old palm, down the dry stream to the fig tree's arms." Ama yawned. "Old songs are boring, Nana!"
text.p07: And off she ran with her best friend Kwesi, a bushbaby with big round eyes. Together they made new paths all over the forest.
text.p08: "This is the swinging way!" said Kwesi. "This is the tunnel way!" said Ama. Every day they found something new, and it was wonderful.
text.p09: Then the dry, dusty wind came. The leaves fell. The fruit was gone. All through the forest, tummies rumbled and the animals grew quiet.
text.p10: Ama tried every new path she knew. Nothing. "Didn't the old ones know a place?" asked Kwesi. Ama frowned. "Three round stones... and... I forget."
text.p11: Ama's cheeks felt hot. Nana had sung that song every single evening, and she had never really listened. She could keep looking for new paths...
text.p12: "No," said Ama. "I'm going back to fetch it." She ran all the way home to the old silkcotton tree. Ka-tum, ka-tum went her heart.
text.p13: "Nana," Ama panted, "please sing me the old path song again. This time, I'll really listen." Nana smiled and tapped her tail. Ka-tum, ka-tum.
text.p14: Ama closed her eyes and listened to every word. "My Nana sang it to me," said Nana softly, "and her Nana sang it to her."
text.p15: Ama hurried back to the hungry animals. "Follow me!" Three round stones: there they were! Then the bent old palm, just like the song said.
text.p16: Down the dry stream they went. But the dust grew so thick that the animals behind her couldn't see where she was going.
text.p17: Then Ama had a new idea. She tapped her tail against her hard scales. Ka-tum, katum! "Follow the beat!" she called.
text.p18: Through the dusty air, everyone followed the sound: the hornbill, the little antelopes, the monkeys, and Kwesi hopping close behind. Ka-tum, ka-tum!
text.p19: At the end of the dry stream, Ama couldn't see the fig tree anywhere. So she climbed a tall tree, up, up, into the treetops.
text.p20: Above the dust, she looked all around. There it was: a giant fig tree with wide, wide arms. "This way!" she called. Ka-tum, ka-tum!
text.p21: Under the wide evening sky stood the old fig tree, heavy with sweet figs. There was plenty for everyone, and busy ants for Ama too.
text.p22: Everyone ate and ate until their tummies were round. "The old song was right!" said Kwesi. "Yes," said Ama, "and it's still right now."
text.p23: Back home, Ama turned the old song into a brand-new clapping game, and all the little ones learned it. Nana tapped along. Ka-tum, ka-tum.
text.p24: Old songs and new games went together now. It's never too late to go back for what you left behind. The End
text.cover: The Old Path Song. A Story About Learning From Those Who Came Before
